title: The price of calm
hook: spilled oil, stolen wine: say, this is what peace of mind costs (Enchiridion 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Job, and I gave it back. Your line was care for it like an inn. Did you try the other verb when you were about to say I lost it? Day three hundred forty-four.

Somebody at work ate your yogurt from the office fridge. Your name was on it. In marker. You could spend the afternoon on this. Draft the passive-aggressive note. Investigate. Tell three people. Or you could do some quick math. The yogurt cost about a dollar. The afternoon of stewing costs a lot more. Epictetus did this math with olive oil and wine. Section twelve of the handbook puts a price tag on peace of mind, and the surprise is how cheap it is. Today: the price of calm.
screen: `THE STOLEN YOGURT.` → `THE AFTERNOON OF STEWING.` → `A PRICE TAG ON PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the bargain. If you want to make progress, Epictetus says, drop thoughts like: if I don't watch my affairs, I'll have nothing to live on. Better, he says bluntly, to die of hunger free of grief and fear than to live in plenty and be troubled. That's strong, and he means it as a direction, not a test. Second, the kitchen. Begin with small things, he says. A little oil spilled. A little wine stolen. Say to yourself: this is the price of tranquility, the price of being undisturbed. Nothing is had for nothing. Third, the word. Tranquility here translates ataraxia: a, not, and a root meaning stirred up. Unstirred, like a pond on a still morning. Fourth, the servant, and an honest note. Epictetus finishes with a household scene: you call your servant and he may not come, or may come and do the wrong thing. He isn't so important, Epictetus says, that it's in his power to disturb you. Epictetus' examples come from a world where owning people was ordinary, and he had been enslaved himself. We can notice that plainly and still take the point that travels: other people's choices aren't a lever on your calm unless you hand it to them. So the yogurt. A dollar. That's the price. Paid gladly, it buys an afternoon back. Small days, small prices: a spilled cup here, a small unfairness there. The expensive part is refusing to pay.
screen: `BETTER HUNGRY THAN TROUBLED.` · `SPILLED OIL, STOLEN WINE.` · `ATARAXIA: UNSTIRRED.` · `NOBODY ELSE HOLDS THE LEVER.` · then, large: `THE PRICE OF CALM.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small within reach: a coin, a pen, a paper clip. Let it stand for one annoyance from today or yesterday. A spill, a late delivery, a parking ticket, the yogurt. Hold it in your palm and name its price, out loud or inside: this is what calm costs. A dollar, five minutes, a little pride. Then set the object down, the way you'd put coins on a counter. Paid. Sit with what you bought. The bell holds the time.
Ataraxia, tranquility, the state of staying undisturbed: a little spilled oil, a little stolen wine, the small price of calm. Nothing is had for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: nothing is had for nothing. When a small loss comes today, let it go cheaply, pay the price, and move on. Day three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat small losses and annoyances as the price of tranquility, naming the cost and letting it go rather than stewing.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 12: tranquility, the state of being unstirred.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't sweat the small stuff.
what it means: every small loss is a price, and paying it gladly buys tranquility.
what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 12 pairs apatheia and ataraxia, freedom from passion and from disturbance, as what the spilled oil buys.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): removed the invented 'his own kitchen, two thousand years earlier'; 'go hungry' corrected to the text's 'die of hunger'; cut the unsourced claim about Epicureans and Skeptics (and its myth item); 'most days' softened; practice changed so it no longer repeats day 343's 'think of one small loss'.

Enchiridion 12 paraphrased (better to die of hunger free of grief and fear; spilled oil, stolen wine, 'this is the price of apatheia, of ataraxia; nothing is got for nothing'; the slave who may not come). Confirm.
Greek ἀταραξία (a- + ταράσσω): confirm; and that both ἀπάθεια and ἀταραξία appear in the passage.
Ataraxia as a shared ideal of Epicureans and Pyrrhonist Skeptics: standard; confirm phrasing.
Slavery: Epictetus' 'slave boy' (παῖς) is rendered 'servant' in the voice with an explicit note that he means an enslaved person; a Keeper may prefer 'slave' outright.
The yogurt scene is an illustration.
